newsitem.title: USA: Childless women who miscarry prone to depression.
newsitem.headline: Childless women who miscarry prone to depression.

text.p: The trauma of miscarriage can make women prone to a major bout of depression, especially women with no children, researchers said on Tuesday.

A study conducted by the New York State Psychiatric Institute in New York City found that 25 of 229 women, or 11 percent, who had miscarried experienced an episode of major depression within the following six months, more than double the proportion in a control group.

The risk of major depression was five times higher among childless women who miscarried compared to the control group, while the likelihood was only slightly higher among miscarrying women who alread had children.

"The presence of children reduces women's risk for depressive illness associated with the bereavement of miscarriage. Whether this benefit extends to other bereavements, such as widowhood, merits study," Richard Neugebauer wrote in an article published in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
The unanticipated physical trauma of losing a future child disrupts a couple's family planning and may create damaging doubts in the woman's mind about her ability to procreate, Neugebauer wrote.
In the United States, about 500,000 women miscarry annually, accounting for between 10 percent and 20 percent of all pregnancies.
The study's control group was made up of 230 women who had not been pregnant. Ten of these women, or 4.3 percent, suffered from depression during the study period.
Another risk factor for depression after a miscarriage were depressive episodes prior to the pregnancy, the study found.
Neugebauer recommended that physicians closely monitor patients who miscarry for several weeks afterward and refer those that become depressed to a mental health professional.

"Additional research is required to determine the duration of increased risk among childless women and to determine whether some groups, (such as) older women, experience a delayed increase in risk," Neugebauer wrote.
